_meta.model: claude-sonnet-4-6 (MODELS.SMART), 2 parallel calls (arc + mechanics) merged, + 1 FAST v2 guard check/repair, + a 10s keep-alive heartbeat
_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden party-architect). PARTY ARCHITECT REWRITE INSTRUCTIONS pass, 2026-09-05: full schema replacement. Old schema (energy_curve, mixing_strategies, conversation_starters, food_and_drink_strategy, music_plan, the_exit, budget_breakdown, disaster_prevention) is GONE — do not resurrect those keys. New: event_read{what_matters,design_priority}, event_shape (pacing STRATEGY, never a feelings prediction), timeline[]{time,phase,action,host_job,why,adjust_if} with RELATIVE time offsets only (Arrival/+20 min/Around halfway/Final 45 min — never a clock time, since this form collects no start time), helping_people_connect[] (was mixing_strategies, 0-3, no forced count), conversation_catalysts[] (0-3), food_and_drink{format,timing,dietary_considerations,special_touch} (dietary_considerations must be procedural — 'identify/separate/label' — never a safety ASSURANCE like 'will keep guests safe'), music{show,arrival,later,wind_down} (show=false + empty fields when irrelevant), budget_priorities{approach,protect_spending_on[],keep_secondary[],use_what_you_have[]} (priorities, never a fabricated total or a 'budget is workable' verdict), things_to_plan_for[] (was disaster_prevention, 0-4, grounded only in supplied facts, never a predicted future event), wind_down{signals[],script} (top-level — DIFFERENT from music.wind_down, which is about lowering volume). Uses router.outputStandard='v2' + runOutputGuard (prohibit/require list) instead of the old bare toArray()-coerce with no guard. IMPORTANT GOTCHA FIXED THIS PASS: the guard's own repair sometimes blanks a flagged field to '' when it can't produce a clean rewrite (observed live on conversation_catalysts and budget_priorities.protect_spending_on) — outputGuard's requiredNonEmpty only protects a fixed known-in-advance path, not a dynamically-indexed array item, so party-architect.js adds its own pruneEmpties() pass AFTER the guard to drop any blanked plain-string array item or object-array item whose primary field (how/plan/action+host_job) came back blank. DO NOT remove pruneEmpties — it is the only thing standing between a guard repair and a visible blank line/empty bullet in production. Case 1 (housewarming) is a guard PASS with zero violations on this run — case 2 (40th birthday) exercises a guard FAIL-then-repair cycle (7 fields, all successfully rewritten with real content, none needed pruning on this particular run, but the dietary_considerations field is the reference for the 'never a safety assurance' fix — compare it against the pre-fix version in git history, which said a labeling setup 'will keep guests safe'). Frontend Recent Plans is a NEW store (`party-plans`, full inputs+plan+date) — the old `party-history` store (preview-only) stays read-only/legacy, same migration pattern as Small Change Big Difference's Recent Small Changes. GENERAL REASONING & GROUNDING RULES pass (2026-09-05, second same-day pass): SHARED_PROMPT was fully replaced (not appended to) with a 25-section grounding spec supplied whole by the user — output schema, arc/mechanics split, and each half's own schema-mechanics (item counts, field names) are UNCHANGED. Both cases re-recorded against the new prompt (output content differs from the prior baseline; structure does not). Also added this same day: a keep-alive heartbeat in the route handler (res.write(' ') every 10s while the two parallel generations + guard run) after a live report of "NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource" at 43s on a non-streaming request — this tool already had documented history of tripping a browser/proxy idle-timeout at this shape (the original pre-split version measured ~82s). Verified: (1) the heartbeat's leading whitespace bytes don't break JSON.parse/response.json() — confirmed via a real browser test, not just Node's http client; (2) an error occurring AFTER the heartbeat has already committed the HTTP status to 200 is still surfaced correctly, via a matching change in src/hooks/useClaudeAPI.js's callToolEndpoint (checks for a bare single-key {error} body even on a 200 response) — verified with a temporary forced-error test exercising exactly that path, then reverted. DO NOT remove the keep-alive or the useClaudeAPI.js check together — removing one without the other reopens either the timeout bug or the silent-blank-result bug.

input.whoIsComing: Three couples from my old job, my brother, and the neighbours from downstairs who I have spoken to twice. Nobody knows anybody outside their own pair.
input.space: One-bed flat. Living room seats five if two people take the floor. Kitchen is a corridor. No outdoor space.
input.constraints: Building has a noise rule after 10pm and thin floors. Nine people is already more than the room comfortably holds.

helping_people_connect.how: When each pair arrives, name them and add one brief, true detail you know about them — their connection to you, something they do, something relevant. Keep it to one sentence per person.
helping_people_connect.when: As each pair arrives, before they settle.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: With nine people in a small flat and no shared history outside their own pair, a brief anchor gives people a genuine starting point rather than leaving them to guess at each other.

helping_people_connect.idea: Seat the neighbours near someone you can connect them to.
helping_people_connect.how: When the neighbours arrive, steer them toward a spot near one of the other pairs and make a brief introduction — even something as simple as 'you both live nearby' or a shared detail you actually know.
helping_people_connect.when: When the neighbours arrive, before the room fills.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: They have the thinnest connection to the group, so giving them an early anchor reduces the chance they spend the evening only talking to each other or to you.

conversation_catalysts: Put a few things out that belong to the flat and invite comment — a plant, a print, a shelf of objects. New home, new space: people have a natural opening to ask what something is or where it came from.

If you moved from somewhere else or have a strong opinion about the neighbourhood, mention it early. 'First thing I noticed about this building was the floors' is the kind of specific that invites the neighbours to respond and pulls others in.

food_and_drink.format: Grazing, not served. With nine people and a corridor kitchen and a room that seats five, you need food that works without a table, without plates that require both hands, and without a moment that stops the room. Finger food, small bites, things that live on a surface and stay there.
food_and_drink.timing: Have food out from the start. Arriving guests have something to do immediately, and it removes any pressure on you to produce a serving moment from a kitchen you cannot host in.
food_and_drink.special_touch: One drink you make in a batch ahead of time — a simple punch, a cold brew situation, a jug of something — so you are not playing bartender all night from a corridor.

music.arrival: Something low-key and melodic that sits under conversation without demanding attention. Quiet enough that people do not raise their voices to talk across the room.
music.later: Keep it roughly the same — with thin floors and a small space, volume is a real constraint throughout, not just near the end. Resist the pull to turn it up as the evening warms.
music.wind_down: Lower it a notch in the final stretch. No sudden change — just enough that the room feels quieter without anyone noticing a decision was made.

budget_priorities.approach: With $120 and nine people, protect the things guests actually encounter — food and something to drink — and treat everything else as secondary. A flat that is clearly a new home needs almost no decoration to read as a housewarming.
protect_spending_on: Enough food that grazing works for three hours without running dry.
A few drink options, including at least one non-alcoholic one that is not just tap water.
Any one batch drink or small special touch you want to offer.
keep_secondary: Decorations — the flat itself is the occasion.
Anything that requires equipment or setup you do not already own.
use_what_you_have: If you already have serving boards or flat surfaces that can hold food, use those rather than buying platters.
If you have a speaker or small device that plays music, that is enough — the room is small.
If you have glasses or mugs in enough quantity, a mismatched set is fine and means nothing to buy.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Nine people in a room that seats five means some guests will be standing or on the floor for stretches of the evening.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide before guests arrive where standing and floor spots are — clear those areas deliberately, not as an afterthought. If you have cushions, a folded blanket, or anything that makes floor-sitting more comfortable, put it there on purpose so it reads as a choice rather than an overflow.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The noise rule and thin floors are active constraints, not just a late-evening concern.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Keep music at conversation volume from the start so you are not managing a gradual creep upward. Nine people in a small flat generate real ambient noise without any music at all.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The corridor kitchen means you cannot restock or prepare anything mid-party without disappearing from the room.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Have everything you need out or reachable before guests arrive. Batch the drink, pre-arrange the food, and set a low threshold for when to top something up so you do it once, not repeatedly.

things_to_plan_for.issue: The neighbours are the most loosely connected guests and also the ones you will continue to live near after the party.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Make a small plan for how to include them early — even one warm introduction on arrival goes a long way, and if the evening ends awkwardly it is harder to undo in a building you share.

event_read.what_matters: Nine people who mostly don't know each other, in a flat that comfortably holds fewer than nine — the real design problem is managing density and noise without making the evening feel managed. The neighbours from downstairs are a specific consideration: they share the floor and the noise rule applies both ways.
event_read.design_priority: Keep the gathering comfortable and low-pressure so nobody feels squeezed or obligated to perform for strangers.

output.event_shape: Let the first stretch do the heaviest social work passively — food and drinks available immediately so there is no waiting around and no moment where guests are standing empty-handed watching the host fuss. The middle of the evening needs nothing added; if conversation is working, that is the plan. One brief shared moment — something that marks the occasion without requiring participation — gives the evening a shape without adding structure. Wind-down is honest and clear, not engineered.

timeline.action: Have drinks and something to eat accessible from the moment the first guest walks in. No serving moment — guests help themselves.
timeline.host_job: Welcome people, take coats if needed, point people toward drinks and food, make quick introductions between anyone standing near each other.
timeline.why: Removes the dead time between arrival and the party feeling started. Guests who arrive into an already-accessible setup have something immediate to do.

timeline.action: Nothing new to introduce. Let the room run. If you have not yet introduced the downstairs neighbours to anyone, do it now — a simple connection to one of the couples is enough.
timeline.host_job: Move between the groups that have formed. You do not need to merge them — just make sure nobody is isolated.
timeline.why: The downstairs neighbours are the pair least likely to have a ready conversation partner. A light introduction early costs almost nothing and avoids them spending the evening only talking to each other.
timeline.adjust_if: If conversation is already crossing between groups without your help, stay out of it.

timeline.action: Do one brief thing that marks the occasion — a short toast, a thank-you to everyone for coming, or whatever fits you. Keep it under a minute. You do not need a speech.
timeline.host_job: Initiate it, keep it short, then immediately return the room to conversation.
timeline.why: A housewarming with nine people who mostly don't know each other benefits from one moment that briefly makes it one group rather than several clusters. It does not need to be elaborate.
timeline.adjust_if: If the room is mid-conversation and the moment would interrupt something that is clearly working, skip it or wait a natural break.

timeline.action: Continue as before. Replenish food and drinks if needed. No new activities.
timeline.host_job: Relax. Stop managing the room and be a guest at your own party.
timeline.why: The plan has done its setup work. The evening should run on its own at this point.

timeline.action: Stop introducing anything new. Do not open more food or drink that signals the evening is extending. Light tidying in the kitchen is fine if it happens naturally.
timeline.host_job: Be present but let conversations conclude at their own pace. Begin saying genuine goodbyes to anyone who indicates they are leaving.
timeline.why: The noise constraint and the duration you planned both point to a clear ending. Winding down early enough avoids a rushed finish near the noise cutoff.
timeline.adjust_if: If guests are already wrapping up on their own, do nothing — just let it happen.

timeline.action: Say clearly that the evening is wrapping up. Use the script below. Thank people individually as they leave.
timeline.host_job: Be the one who names the ending — do not leave guests guessing whether the party is over.
timeline.why: With thin floors and a noise rule, clarity serves everyone including the neighbours directly below.

signals: Say directly that the evening is wrapping up — no behavioral hints, just the words.
Thank people individually as they head for the door rather than as a group announcement.
wind_down.script: Right, I think that is us for the evening — I am so glad you all came. Thank you for helping me break the place in.

input.whoIsComing: Mostly close friends from the last 15 years, a few work people, 3 kids under 10. About a third haven't met each other.
input.space: Backyard with covered patio, fits ~25 standing. Kitchen and living room flow out to it. Late September — should be warm but cool by 9pm.
input.constraints: Two guests have tree nut allergies, one is gluten-free, one is sober (they're fine with others drinking).

helping_people_connect.how: When you greet each arriving guest, point them toward the covered patio or food setup so they have somewhere natural to be. If you happen to know two people could connect over something specific, make that introduction — otherwise let people settle at their own pace.
helping_people_connect.when: During arrival, while you are still near the entrance and guests are trickling in.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: About a third of 22 guests have not met, and the covered patio gives you a natural gathering point to direct people toward without forcing a group activity.

helping_people_connect.idea: A loose display that gives people something to react to.
helping_people_connect.how: If you already have photos, objects, or a playlist from the last 15 years, put them somewhere visible — a table, a surface, a screen. No labels or instructions needed.
helping_people_connect.when: In place before guests arrive, available throughout.
helping_people_connect.why_it_fits: A shared reference point gives guests who do not know each other something specific to comment on without needing a prompt from the host.

conversation_catalysts: A small card or chalkboard near the food asking guests to write one thing they remember or predict about the birthday person — no obligation, but something sitting there invites it.
If the birthday person has a running joke, a favourite team, or a well-known hobby and you have a way to nod to it visibly, that gives people an instant question to ask someone who knows them well.

food_and_drink.format: Grazing format — food available continuously across a few surfaces rather than served in a single moment. With 22 people moving between a backyard, patio, kitchen, and living room, grazing lets guests eat without breaking conversations or creating a queue.
food_and_drink.timing: Have food ready and visible from the moment guests arrive. Arriving guests having something to pick up immediately means they do not need to wait for a serving signal, and the food stays available through the cooler part of the evening rather than being tied to a single midpoint moment.
food_and_drink.dietary_considerations: Two guests have tree nut allergies — keep tree nuts entirely out of shared dishes rather than offering a separate option, and if any dish could be cross-contaminated label it clearly. One guest is gluten-free — have at least a few clearly labelled options that are gluten-free by nature rather than adaptation. One guest does not drink — have a non-alcoholic option that stands on its own rather than being an afterthought.
food_and_drink.special_touch: A self-serve drink station — non-alcoholic and alcoholic options side by side — with garnishes guests can add themselves keeps things relaxed and removes the host from drink duty for most of the evening.

music.arrival: Something familiar and easy to talk over — moderate tempo, low enough that guests do not have to raise their voices. The point is atmosphere, not attention.
music.later: If the energy in the space picks up, you can let the volume and tempo rise slightly. If conversation is going well at the same level, leave it alone.
music.wind_down: In the final stretch, bring the volume down gradually so conversation naturally becomes the dominant sound rather than the music.

budget_priorities.approach: With 22 people and several hard dietary constraints, food and drink quality and variety deserve the largest share of the budget — cutting there creates the most visible problems. Everything else is secondary to getting that right.
protect_spending_on: Food — enough variety and quantity for 22 guests, with safe options for the constrained guests built in rather than bolted on.
Drinks — a proper non-alcoholic option alongside whatever else you are offering, not just water.
Any rental or borrowed equipment the space genuinely lacks — seating, a cooler, serving surfaces — before spending on decoration.
keep_secondary: Decorations — a relaxed backyard gathering does not need much, and the space itself does the work.
Party favours or extras — they are the first thing to cut if food and drink costs run high.
use_what_you_have: If you already have a speaker, use it rather than renting anything.
If you have serving platters, bowls, or a cooler, those replace rental costs.
If the kitchen flows naturally to the patio, use it as a serving base rather than buying a separate outdoor table.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Temperature drop late in the evening — you expect it to cool around 9pm.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Decide in advance whether you can keep the covered patio usable as it cools — check whether you have access to a heater or blankets, or plan to move the gathering indoors. Don't improvise when temperature drops.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Three children under 10 in a mostly adult gathering.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Confirm with the adults bringing them whether the children need a designated space, activity, or supervision arrangement — and whether there is somewhere lower-traffic they can settle if the main space gets loud.

things_to_plan_for.issue: Tree nut allergy across shared food.
things_to_plan_for.plan: Before finalising any menu, check every dish and every ingredient label for tree nuts, and decide whether to exclude them from the event entirely or manage by strict labelling — partial measures carry real risk.

things_to_plan_for.issue: 22 guests in a space that fits roughly 25 standing.
things_to_plan_for.plan: If the kitchen and living room are usable overflow, plan for guests to spread into them naturally — having food or seating in more than one area helps the patio avoid feeling packed.

event_read.what_matters: About a third of 22 guests don't know each other, and the group includes kids, dietary constraints, and a natural temperature shift around the later part of the evening — so the design needs to make it easy for strangers to connect without engineering it, and to stay comfortable as conditions change. The sober guest and dietary constraints need to be handled invisibly in the setup so no one feels singled out.
event_read.design_priority: Keep the host out of management mode so the gathering can run on its own energy, with one deliberate birthday moment as the only required intervention.

output.event_shape: The plan runs in three loose phases: an unhurried arrival window where food, drinks, and the space itself do the work; an open middle stretch where conversation carries the event without host involvement; and one brief, optional shared birthday moment that can be skipped if the room doesn't need it. The final stretch tapers naturally toward the end time rather than being pushed. The host's only active jobs are welcoming people, making a few introductions when a genuine connection exists, initiating the one shared moment, and signaling the close.

timeline.action: Set out all food, non-alcoholic drinks, and clearly labeled options before anyone walks in. Arrange the covered patio and indoor areas so guests can move freely between them without being directed.
timeline.host_job: Finish setup, then stop setting up. Be available at the entry point to welcome people as they arrive.
timeline.why: Removing the first-drink and first-food friction means arriving guests can settle immediately without waiting on the host or hunting for anything.

timeline.action: Let arrivals unfold at their own pace. Make introductions only when you know a specific reason two people would find each other interesting — not as a general policy.
timeline.host_job: Greet people, point out food and drinks, make the occasional targeted introduction, and resist the urge to organize the room.
timeline.why: Early structure at a relaxed gathering often works against itself. People finding their own footing is part of the chill vibe.
timeline.adjust_if: If someone arrives alone and hasn't met others yet, a single warm introduction to one person nearby is enough — no need to do more.

timeline.action: Check that food is still accessible and drinks are stocked. If anything needs refreshing, handle it now rather than mid-party.
timeline.host_job: A quick practical pass through the setup — then rejoin the gathering as a guest, not a host.
timeline.why: This is likely when most expected guests have arrived and the gathering is in full motion. Getting ahead of any supply gaps now avoids interrupting the open middle.
timeline.adjust_if: If people are still arriving in numbers, hold off on the shared moment below until arrivals have slowed.

timeline.action: Initiate one brief shared birthday moment — a toast, a dessert, a song, or something else that fits the person being celebrated. Keep it short. Let it end naturally and let the party continue.
timeline.host_job: Call the moment, lead it, and get out of the way once it's done. No speeches required unless someone genuinely wants to give one.
timeline.why: A 40th birthday warrants one point where the gathering acknowledges the occasion together. Placing it around the midpoint means everyone has likely arrived and there's still plenty of evening left afterward.
timeline.adjust_if: If conversation is running well and the room feels cohesive, it's fine to let this moment arrive a little later. If it feels forced, make it very brief. If the birthday person would prefer to skip it entirely, skip it.

timeline.action: Nothing new. Let the gathering continue under its own momentum.
timeline.host_job: Be a guest at your own party. The plan is working if you don't have much to do right now.
timeline.why: Introducing new activities or prompts in the back half of a relaxed gathering typically disrupts rather than improves it.
timeline.adjust_if: If the kids are getting restless or tired, having a quieter indoor space available for them — and whoever is with them — may help without affecting the main gathering.

timeline.action: Stop introducing anything new. Consolidate remaining food rather than replenishing. If music is playing, no need to change it, but don't add energy.
timeline.host_job: Be present and warm, but begin letting the evening find its own close. No announcements needed yet.
timeline.why: The temperature may be dropping by this point, which will naturally prompt some guests to think about leaving. The setup should support that rather than fight it.

timeline.action: Thank guests directly as they begin to leave. If the event needs a clearer close, say it plainly — see wind-down script.
timeline.host_job: Give genuine goodbyes. Light, visible tidying is fine if it's already happening naturally.
timeline.why: A clear, warm close is better than a party that trails off without acknowledgment.

signals: Consolidate food — stop replenishing and bring remaining items together rather than leaving stations spread out.
If the temperature has dropped noticeably, do not set up heat sources or move the party inside — let the natural shift do its work.
Begin saying genuine goodbyes to guests who are leaving rather than encouraging them to stay.
wind_down.script: This was such a great night — I'm so glad everyone was here for this one. Safe travels home, and thank you for coming.
